content:
Quick answer: The NHS says recovery from a hip replacement can take several months, and it varies with your age and general health. You need crutches or a walking frame at first. Wait at least 6 weeks before driving, and only drive when your doctor agrees you are fit to drive. Return to work when you feel ready: that is often about 6 weeks, and it depends on the job. These are descriptions from NHS advice, not a promise about your operation. Follow your surgical team.

This page summarises current NHS advice on recovering from a hip replacement and on complications that need urgent help. It is general information for people in the UK. Your surgeon, physiotherapist and occupational therapist know the approach used in your operation. If their advice differs from the ranges below, follow theirs.

What happens in the first days after a hip replacement?

After surgery you spend some time in a recovery room, and you are given pain relief. The hip will be sore. Nurses and physiotherapists help you start walking as soon as possible, using crutches or a walking frame at first. The NHS says you can usually go home when the wound is healing and you can get around safely. If you are generally fit and the surgery went well, that is often around 1 to 3 days after the operation. Before you leave, a physiotherapist or occupational therapist should talk with you about daily activities and a home exercise programme. Doing those exercises early is part of how strength and movement return. It is not a race to drop the walking aid.

How should you use walking aids after a hip replacement?

The NHS says you will need crutches or a walking frame at first, and that you should walk every day as far as is comfortable. Talk to your physiotherapist if walking is a problem. There is no single week when everyone can stop using a walking aid. Progress depends on pain, balance, the operation and the plan your team gave you. Do not treat a week number you have read elsewhere as a date you must hit.

Is pain and swelling normal after a hip replacement?

The NHS says some pain and swelling in the legs and feet is usual, and that these symptoms usually improve over a few weeks. You are usually given pain relief to help. A nurse takes out stitches or clips after about 10 days. A follow-up appointment is often around 6 to 12 weeks to check how you are recovering. Sitting still for a long time can make swelling worse. The NHS suggests a reclining position at times, and also getting up to move.

What does the NHS say about driving after a hip replacement?

The NHS says wait at least 6 weeks to drive, and check with your doctor that you are fit to drive. That is a minimum in the general advice, not a date your insurer or your surgeon has already approved. Do not drive until the clinician looking after your hip says you can. Ask them what they need to see before that, and tell your insurer.

When can you go back to work after a hip replacement?

The NHS says return to work when you feel ready. That often takes about 6 weeks, and it depends on the type of work you do. A desk job and a job on your feet are not the same decision. Agree a plan with your surgical team and, if you have one, occupational health. Keep walking within what is comfortable, and keep doing the exercises your physiotherapist recommended.

Which hip precautions apply in the early weeks?

NHS recovery advice tells people not to:

  • sit with their legs crossed
  • bend the hip more than 90 degrees (a right angle)
  • bend down to touch their feet or ankles
  • sit on a low chair or toilet seat, or a chair without arms
  • do exercises that involve jumping, sudden turns, or a high risk of falling while the hip is recovering
  • lift or move heavy objects until they are told it is safe

Your team may add or relax precautions because of the way your hip was replaced. Their written advice is the one to follow.

Which symptoms after a hip replacement need urgent help?

The NHS complications page says a hip replacement is a common operation, and that it still has risks. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111 if you have recently had a hip replacement and you have throbbing or cramping pain in the hip or leg, a high temperature or you feel hot, cold or shivery, oozing or pus from the wound, or redness, tenderness, swelling or pain in the hip or leg that is not getting better or is getting worse. The NHS says these could be signs of infection or a blood clot.

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have pain and swelling in the hip or leg and you are having difficulty breathing or chest pain. The NHS says that could be a blood clot in the lungs and needs immediate treatment.

The NHS pages used here were last reviewed on 6 March 2024, with a next review due on 6 March 2027. Check them if you want the current wording, and ask your surgical team about your own recovery.

Frequently asked questions

How long will I need crutches or a walking frame after hip replacement?

The NHS says you need crutches or a walking frame at first, and that you should walk each day only as far as is comfortable. It does not give a week when everyone can stop. Your physiotherapist decides that with you. Do not treat any range of weeks as a promise.

When can I drive after a hip replacement?

The NHS says wait at least 6 weeks, and check with your doctor that you are fit to drive. Six weeks is the earliest point in that general advice, not permission for your operation. Do not drive until the clinician looking after you agrees, and check with your insurer.

When can I return to work after a hip replacement?

The NHS says go back when you feel ready. That often takes about 6 weeks and depends on the type of work. Agree the timing with your surgical team. A physical job may take longer than a seated one.

What movements should I avoid in the early weeks?

NHS advice says not to cross your legs, bend the hip past a right angle, reach down to your feet or ankles, use a low seat or a chair without arms, or do jumping, sudden turns or exercises with a high risk of falling. Do not lift heavy objects until you are told it is safe. Your own team may give different precautions. Follow those.

How long does it take to recover from a hip replacement?

The NHS says it may take several months, and that this varies with age and general health. A follow-up is often around 6 to 12 weeks. Pain and swelling often ease over a few weeks, but that is not the same as being fully recovered. Your surgical team’s milestones matter more than a calendar.

When should I get urgent help after a hip replacement?

Contact your GP urgently or NHS 111 if the wound is oozing, you have a high temperature or shivers, or pain, redness or swelling in the hip or leg is worsening. Call 999 or go to A&E if you also have chest pain or difficulty breathing. The NHS says these can be signs of infection or a blood clot.

key_takeaways: Recovery usually takes several months and varies with age and general health, so follow your surgical team's plan rather than a fixed timetable.
Use crutches or a walking frame at first, and walk every day as far as is comfortable.
Wait at least 6 weeks before driving, and only drive when your doctor says you are fit to.
Call 999 if pain and swelling in the hip or leg come with chest pain or difficulty breathing.
